claim: Active matter systems can generate highly ordered structures by consuming energy at the level of individual constituents.
source: Active matter systems can generate highly ordered structures, avoiding equilibrium through the consumption of energy by individual constituents.
evidence: This is a general statement about active matter systems presented in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cytoskeleton is organized into structures such as the mitotic spindle through the coordinated activity of many motor proteins walking along microtubules.
source: in cells, the cytoskeleton is organized into structures such as the mitotic spindle through the coordinated activity of many motor proteins walking along microtubules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular organization cited as background.

claim: Aster size depends on the motor used to create the aster.
source: We demonstrate that aster size depends on the motor used to create the aster
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Network contraction rates scale linearly with the single-motor speed in quasi-one-dimensional contraction experiments.
source: we show that network contraction rates scale linearly with the single-motor speed in quasi-one-dimensional contraction experiments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Many motor proteins exist in nature with a variety of properties such as speeds, stall and detachment forces, processivities, and directionalities.
source: The motor-microtubule system is an excellent system in which to test this question, as many motor proteins with a variety of properties, such as speeds, stall and detachment forces, processivities, and directionalities, exist in nature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor protein diversity.

claim: Motor proteins play a variety of roles in cells including transporting cargo and localizing to distinct regions of the mitotic spindle.
source: These motors play a variety of roles in cells; some transport cargo while others localize to distinct regions of the mitotic spindle (Wickstead and Gull, 2006; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Endow et al., 1994; Pavin and Tolić, 2021; Anjur-Dietrich et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Kinesin-1's high speed and processivity make it excellent at transporting cargo.
source: For example, kinesin-1s high speed and processivity make it excellent at transporting cargo (Grover et al., 2016; Hirokawa et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by literature citations.

claim: Kinesin-1 tetramers can form asters, extensile networks, and contractile networks in vitro.
source: However, in in vitro systems, kinesin-1 tetramers are able to form asters, extensile networks, and contractile networks (Surrey et al., 2001; Sanchez et al., 2012; DeCamp et al., 2015; Ross et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Ncd (kinesin-14) and Kif11 (kinesin-5) have been shown to form asters in vitro.
source: Ncd (kinesin-14) and Kif11 (kinesin-5) have similarly been shown to form asters in vitro, yet it remains unclear how the properties of these motors affect the structure and dynamics of the assemblies created (Surrey et al., 2001; Sanchez et al., 2012; DeCamp et al., 2015; Ross et al., 2019; Roostalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by literature citations.

claim: An optogenetic in vitro motor-microtubule system demonstrated the formation of asters and other contractile networks with kinesin-1 (K401) upon light activation.
source: Our recently developed optogenetic in vitro motor-microtubule system demonstrated the formation of asters and other contractile networks with kinesin-1 (K401) upon light activation (Ross et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a literature citation to prior work.

claim: In the optogenetic system, K401 motors are fused to light-dimerizable proteins such that in the presence of light the optogenetic pair bind, acting as a crosslink between microtubules.
source: Briefly, we fused K401 motors to an optogenetic pair of light-dimerizable proteins, such that in the presence of light the optogenetic pair bind, acting as a crosslink between microtubules that the motor heads are walking along.
evidence: This describes the experimental system design.

claim: The optogenetic system enabled formation of microtubule structures with spatiotemporal control by illuminating regions of the sample at will.
source: Previously, we showed that this scheme enabled us to form microtubule structures with spatiotemporal control by illuminating regions of the sample at will.
evidence: This refers to prior experimental results.

claim: Light-controlled aster formation with kinesin-5 (Kif11) and kinesin-14 (Ncd) is demonstrated for the first time.
source: We now show how this system can be re-purposed to ask a new set of questions with kinesin-5 (Kif11) and kinesin-14 (Ncd), and form asters of varying sizes with each motor, demonstrating light-controlled aster formation with these motors for the first time.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current work supported by experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: Calculated motor distributions in an aster depend on motor properties and fit with experimental data.
source: We find that calculated motor distributions in an aster depend on the motor properties and fit with our experimental data.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the model and experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Contraction rates in quasi-one-dimensional microtubule networks directly depend on the single-motor velocity.
source: Further, by using motors with different speeds, we find that contraction rates in quasi-one-dimensional microtubule networks directly depend on the single-motor velocity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Kinesin motors are fused to the light-dimerizable pair iLid and micro.
source: In brief, kinesin motors are fused to the light-dimerizable pair iLid and micro.
evidence: This describes the experimental system design.

claim: In the absence of light, motor dimers walk along microtubules but do not organize them.
source: In the absence of light, motor dimers walk along microtubules but do not organize them
evidence: This describes the behavior of the experimental system.

claim: Upon activation with light, motor dimers couple together to form tetramers, crosslinking the microtubules they are walking along.
source: upon activation with light, the motor dimers couple together to form tetramers, crosslinking the microtubules they are walking along as shown in Figure 1A.
evidence: This describes the behavior of the experimental system and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The optogenetic bond lasts for about 20 s before reverting to the undimerized state.
source: The optogenetic bond lasts for about 20 s before reverting to the undimerized state, thus in our experiments, we repeatedly illuminate the sample every 20 s (Guntas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Projecting a cylinder of light on the sample results in the formation of an aster.
source: As demonstrated by Ross et al., projecting a cylinder of light on the sample results in the formation of an aster, and different structures can be formed and manipulated by illumination with different light patterns.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation to prior work.

claim: By varying concentrations of motors and microtubules, it is possible to form multiple smaller asters within the region.
source: However, by varying concentrations of the motors and microtubules, it is possible to form multiple smaller asters within the region, a few examples of which are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: K401 has a speed of approximately 600 nm/s.
evidence: This is measured data from gliding assays as stated in Table 1.

claim: Ncd236 has a speed of approximately 115 nm/s.
source: Ncd236	≈115 nm/s
evidence: This is measured data from gliding assays as stated in Table 1.

claim: Kif11(513) has a speed of approximately 70 nm/s.
evidence: This is measured data from gliding assays as stated in Table 1.

claim: Each of the three motors (K401, Ncd236, Kif11) is able to form asters of varying sizes.
source: As seen in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, each of these motors is able to form asters of varying sizes in our system.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ncd has previously been shown to form asters as constitutive oligomers.
source: although Ncd has previously been shown to form asters as constitutive oligomers (Belmonte et al., 2017; Hentrich and Surrey, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: All three motors were able to form asters upon illumination by various excitation diameters ranging from 50 to 600 μm.
source: We found that all were able to form asters upon illumination by various excitation diameters ranging from 50 to 600 μm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The dynamics of aster formation by these motors roughly scale with the motor speeds.
source: Interestingly, the dynamics of aster formation by these motors seemed to roughly scale with the motor speeds – K401 formed asters the quickest, followed by Ncd236, and Kif11 took the most time to form an aster.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Aster size increases with excitation diameter.
source: We found that aster size increases with excitation diameter, as shown in Figure 1B, D, consistent with what was shown by Ross et al. for K401 (Ross et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, D and a literature citation.

claim: The aster size roughly scaled with the volume of the excitation area, suggesting that the number of microtubules limits the size of the aster.
source: In Ross et al., it was determined that the aster size roughly scaled with the volume of the excitation area, suggesting that the number of microtubules limits the size of the aster.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation and inference from prior work.

claim: For each excitation diameter except 50 μm, K401 formed the largest asters and Ncd formed the smallest, with Kif11 producing asters of intermediate size.
source: Interestingly, we find that the size of the asters also depends on the motor used. For each excitation diameter, except for the 50 μm case, K401 formed the largest asters and Ncd formed the smallest, with Kif11 producing asters of intermediate size (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The trend in aster size correlates with motor processivity, with K401 being the most processive, followed by Kif11, and then Ncd.
source: We found that this trend correlates with motor processivity; K401 is the most processive, followed by Kif11, and then Ncd.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing experimental data with known motor properties.

claim: Intensity of aster formation was related to motor processivity in prior work by Surrey et al., 2001.
source: This is similar to the findings in Surrey et al., 2001, in which intensity of aster formation was related to motor processivity.
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Continuum models were developed for motor-filament mixtures which predicted the radial profile of motors in confined two-dimensional systems.
source: In these studies, continuum models were developed for motor-filament mixtures which predicted the radial profile of motors in confined two-dimensional systems (Nédélec et al., 2001; Lee and Kardar, 2001; Sankararaman et al., 2004; Aranson and Tsimring, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: Asters formed in the current experiments are three-dimensional due to the much larger depth of the flow cells (roughly 100 μm).
source: Additionally, in contrast to the earlier study (Nédélec et al., 2001), asters formed in our experiments are three-dimensional due to the much larger depth of the flow cells (roughly 100 μm), and are thus more similar to the structures observed in cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and compares it to prior work.

claim: The asters are assumed to be radially symmetric outside the central disordered region (aster core).
source: For modeling purposes, then, we consider our asters to be radially symmetric outside the central disordered region (which we refer to as the aster core, as depicted schematically in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on experimental observations.

claim: In the steady state of the system, microtubules on average have no radial movement.
source: In the steady state of the system, which we assume our asters have reached at the end of the experiment, microtubules on average have no radial movement and hence, do not contribute to motor speed.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption validated by FRAP experiments.

claim: FRAP experiments of steady-state asters show little radial flux of the microtubules.
source: To assess the validity of this assumption, we performed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments of steady-state asters, and observe little radial flux of the microtubules, an example is shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The model can capture specific features often seen in measured microtubule profiles, such as the presence of an inflection point.
source: This is unlike the previous models which imposed specific functional forms on the microtubule distribution (e.g., a constant value [Lee and Kardar, 2001; Sankararaman et al., 2004] or a power-law decay [Nédélec et al., 2001]), rendering them unable to capture the specific features often seen in our measured microtubule profiles, such as the presence of an inflection point (see Figure 1C for an example).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the current model over prior models, with reference to data in Figure 1C.

claim: The model fits well to the average motor data for a Kif11 aster.
source: A demonstration of this procedure on an example Kif11 aster is shown in Figure 2D where a good fit to the average motor data can be observed.
evidence: This is supported by the fit shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The fitting error for asters is low.
source: The fitting error for other asters is similarly low (Figure 2E, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for the collection of fitted profiles).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Highly processive movement was observed for clusters of HSET (human kinesin-14).
source: A highly processive movement was similarly observed for clusters of HSET (human kinesin-14) (Norris et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Highly processive movement was observed for plant kinesin-14 motors.
source: and plant kinesin-14 motors (Jonsson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Stalling of motors upon reaching the microtubule ends contributes to reduction in effective speed.
source: One contributor to this reduction is the stalling of motors upon reaching the microtubule ends.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from the model and experimental observations.

claim: Jamming of K401 motors in dense aster regions may contribute to the discrepancy between inferred and estimated λ0.
source: We hypothesize that an additional contribution may come from the jamming of K401 motors in dense aster regions.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from literature and experimental observations.

claim: K401 motors pause when encountering obstructions during their walk.
source: This is motivated by the experiments which showed that K401 motors would pause when encountering obstructions during their walk (Ferro et al., 2019; Schneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations.

claim: The minimal model of motor distributions is able to capture the distinctions in aster structure through motor-specific effective parameters.
source: Overall, our study shows that the minimal model of motor distributions proposed in Figure 2 is able to capture the distinctions in aster structure through motor-specific effective parameters
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model fitting to experimental data.

claim: The distribution of microtubules is generally broader than that of the motors.
source: Our model also provides insights on the observation that the distribution of microtubules is generally broader than that of the motors.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The relative width of the motor distribution compared to the microtubule distribution is fairly constant among asters.
source: We found that the relative width of the motor distribution compared to the microtubule distribution is fairly constant among asters, with their difference being the largest for Ncd motors, consistent with our model predictions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data and model predictions.

claim: Ross et al. demonstrated the formation of quasi-one-dimensional contractile networks by creating two asters that are initially separated by a given distance, then activating a thin rectangular region between them.
source: Ross et al. demonstrated the formation of quasi-one-dimensional contractile networks by creating two asters that are initially separated by a given distance, then activating a thin rectangular region between them to form a network connecting the asters that pulls them together (Ross et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation to prior work.

claim: An increase in maximum aster merger speed with greater initial separation was observed in prior work.
source: In these experiments, an increase in maximum aster merger speed with greater initial separation was observed.
evidence: This refers to observations from prior work (Ross et al., 2019).

claim: A linear increase in contractile speed with distance from the center of the network is observed.
source: Using optical flow to measure the contraction speed throughout the network, we observe a linear increase in contractile speed with distance from the center of the network, as shown in Figure 3b.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The linear relationship between speed and distance suggests that the contractile network can be thought of as a series of connected contractile units.
source: This relationship suggests that the contractile network can be thought of as a series of connected contractile units.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: The findings are in agreement with results from several studies of contractile rates in actomyosin networks that suggested telescoping models of contraction.
source: These findings are in agreement with results from several studies of contractile rates in actomyosin networks, that suggested telescoping models of contraction, and suggest that this may be a common mechanism across cytosketetal networks (Thoresen et al., 2011; Linsmeier et al., 2016; Schuppler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by literature citations and inference.

claim: The ratios of the slopes of the best fit lines for merger speed vs. separation match the ratios of motor speeds.
source: Interestingly, the ratios of the slopes of these lines match the ratios of motor speeds from Table 1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The rate of contraction in the network is set by the motor speed and the increase of network speed with distance is due to adding more connected contractile units.
source: Thus, we conclude that the rate of contraction in the network is set by the motor speed and the increase of network speed with distance is due to adding more connected contractile units (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and inference.

claim: Only the initial contraction rate is measured in the merger experiments, over the first approximately 100 s.
source: It is important to note that we only measure the initial contraction rate in these experiments, over the first ≈100 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental measurement protocol.

claim: On the time scale of approximately 100 s, the network is thought of as an elastic material.
source: On this time scale, we think of the network as an elastic material, since the time for motor unbinding and rearrangement should be longer than this.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on inference about time scales.

claim: The time scale for the optogenetic pair to unbind is about 20 s.
source: The time scale for the optogenetic pair to unbind is about 20 s (Guntas et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The average time for two optogenetic pairs to unbind is about 400 s.
source: since binding events are independent then the average time for two to unbind is about 400 s.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical reasoning.

claim: Processivity is the key control variable for aster size.
source: Our leading hypothesis is that the key control variable is the processivity of the motors.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations.

claim: Surrey et al. found that processivity affected the intensity of aster formation in simulations.
source: Early work by Surrey et al. found that processivity affected the intensity of aster formation in simulations, which may be related to our observations, but to the best of our knowledge no model of this effect has been developed (Surrey et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The parameters inferred from the model in some cases differ from those expected from the single-molecule properties of the motors, indicating that higher-order effects are playing important roles.
source: Interestingly, the parameters we infer in some cases differ from those we would expect from the single-molecule properties of the motors, indicating that higher-order effects such as cooperativity in collections of motors increasing the processivity of the collective, are playing important roles.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing model results with expected values.

claim: Contraction speeds measured in pseudo-one-dimensional networks are related to the single-motor speed.
source: In addition, we measure contraction speeds in pseudo-one-dimensional networks and find that the speeds are related to the single-motor speed.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Human kinesin-5 (Kif11/Eg5) 5–513 was PCR amplified from mCherry-Kinesin11-N-18 plasmid.
source: Human kinesin-5 (Kif11/Eg5) 5–513 was PCR amplified from mCherry-Kinesin11-N-18 plasmid (gift from Michael Davidson, Addgene # 55067).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The Kif11 5-513 fragment was previously shown to form functional dimers.
source: This fragment was previously shown to form functional dimers (Valentine et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Kinesin 1 1–401 (K401) was PCR amplified from pWC2 plasmid.
source: Kinesin 1 1–401 (K401) was PCR amplified from pWC2 plasmid (Addgene # 15960).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Ncd 236–701 was PCR amplified from a plasmid gifted by Andrea Serra-Marques.
source: Ncd 236–701 was PCR amplified from a plasmid gifted by Andrea Serra-Marques.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Protein expression and purification was done in SF9 cells.
source: Protein expression and purification was done in SF9 cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Microtubules were polymerized with 75 μM unlabeled tubulin and 5 μM tubulin-Alexa Fluor 647.
source: In brief, 75 μM unlabeled tubulin (Cytoskeleton) and 5 μM tubulin-Alexa Fluor 647 (Cytoskeleton) were combined with 1 mM DTT and 0.6 mM GMP-CPP in M2B buffer
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: GMP-CPP stabilized microtubules were formed by incubation at 37°C for 1 hr.
source: then the supernatant was incubated at 37°C for 1 hr to form GMP-CPP stabilized microtubules.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Experiments were run with Micro-Manager, running custom scripts to control pattern projection and stage movement.
source: Experiments were run with Micro-Manager (Edelstein et al., 2010), running custom scripts to controlled pattern projection and stage movement.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and cites the software used.

claim: After an hour of activation, a z-stack of the microtubule and motor fluorescence throughout the depth of the flow chamber was taken at 5 μm increments in each position.
source: After an hour of activation, a z-stack of the microtubule and motor fluorescence throughout the depth of the flow chamber was taken at 5 μm increments in each position.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Motor speeds were determined by gliding assay.
source: Motor speeds were determined by gliding assay.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Individual microtubules were tracked using custom-written Python code to determine their speed.
source: Individual microtubules were tracked using custom-written Python code to determine their speed.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.

claim: The asters have centers that are very dense with motors and microtubules.
source: We observe that the asters we create have centers that are very dense with motors and microtubules.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: By fluorescence microscopy, organized aster arms are not observed in the dense central region.
source: By fluorescence microscopy, we do not observe organized aster arms in this region and hypothesized that the microtubules are disordered in this region.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: When imaged with a Pol-Scope, the arms of the asters are bright, indicating high alignment.
source: When imaged with a Pol-Scope, the arms of our asters are bright, indicating high alignment, and their azimuthal angle confirms that they are radially symmetric around the center (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The center of the aster is dark in Pol-Scope imaging, which is interpreted to mean that this region is disordered.
source: The center of the aster is dark, which we interpret to mean that this region is disordered.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data.

claim: A disordered center may result from steric hindrance due to a high density of microtubules in that region.
source: A disordered center may be a result from steric hindrance due to a high density of microtubules in that region, which prevents the motors from aligning the microtubules.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: FRAP experiments show there is little to no net radial movement of the microtubules, and slow angular motion.
source: From these images, it is clear that there is little to no net radial movement of the microtubules, and slow angular motion.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: For the smallest asters, the aster size can be larger than the illumination region.
source: It can be seen in these images that for the smallest asters, the aster size can be larger than the illumination region.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Diffusion of dimerized motors outside of the activation region allows them to bind microtubules in the background region and incorporate them into the asters.
source: We believe this is due to diffusion of dimerized motors outside of the activation region, where they can bind microtubules in the background region and incorporate them into the asters.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: For larger excitation diameters, the microtubules in the activated region get concentrated in the aster, leaving a region depleted of microtubules between the aster and the background region.
source: For larger excitation diameters, the microtubules in the activated region get concentrated in the aster, leaving a region depleted of microtubules between the aster and the background region.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The outer radius of the aster is defined as the radius at which the median microtubule fluorescence is twice the background fluorescence.
source: We chose to define the outer radius of the aster as the radius at which the median microtubule fluorescence is twice the background fluorescence.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.
